name: Latency Budgets and Streaming
question: Where do the seconds go before users see anything?
summary: Set a user-facing budget for the whole request, such as first words within 3 s and the full answer within 5.5 s at p95, then measure p50 and p95 for every stage and change the shape of the request until it fits. The main levers sit in your application, not the model server: stream status and tokens, run independent calls in parallel, cut sequential LLM hops, use a faster model for early steps, and put a timeout with a planned fallback on each slow dependency. Serving-level speed-ups such as prefix caching and speculative decoding shorten individual stages; this technique decides which stages to shorten and what the user sees while they run.
useCases: Chat and support assistants where users leave if the screen stays blank
Agents that chain several LLM calls, tools and retrieval before answering
Launch reviews where a product owner asks for a latency target in writing

items.detail: targets for first visible text, first answer words and total time, set at p95
p50 and p95 per stage: each LLM call, tool and retrieval
the chain of waits that sets the total; only shortening it helps
a status line early, then answer tokens as they are generated
each sequential model call adds its own first-token and generation time
a cap on each slow dependency and a planned, labelled degraded answer

steps: Write the budget as p95 targets for first words and total time
Trace every stage and record p50 and p95, not averages
Remove waits: parallel independent calls, merge or shrink LLM hops, stream early
Cap slow dependencies with timeouts and count the answers that fall back
pitfalls: Budgeting on p50 alone: the slow 5% is where users leave
A timeout so tight that a fifth of answers quietly degrade
Streaming a blank-looking wait, such as a spinner with no status, and calling it solved
remember: Budget the p95, not the average. Show something early, wait on less.
caption: Illustrative: Tejas Trade, a fictional stockbroking app, answering “why did my order fail?”.

steps.title: Write the budget down
steps.text: Tejas Trade, a fictional stockbroking app, sets two p95 targets for “why did my order fail?”: the first words of the answer within 3.0 s and the whole answer within 5.5 s. p95 means 95 of every 100 users get at least this; averages hide the slow ones who leave.

steps.title: Measure every stage
steps.text: Wrap each stage in a span and keep p50 and p95. The first trace: intent call 600 / 900 ms, three tools in turn 1,550 / 3,400 ms, retrieval 150 / 200 ms, answer call 2,400 / 3,200 ms. Total 4,700 ms at p50 and 7,700 ms at p95, with a blank screen throughout.

steps.title: Show something early
steps.text: A status line goes out at once, about 0.3 s after the tap, and the answer streams token by token. The user now sees words when the first token arrives, 500 ms into the answer call, instead of after all 2,400 ms.

steps.title: Wait on less: run tools together
steps.text: Order status (300 ms), margin check (450 ms) and the exchange rejection log (800 ms) do not need each other, so gather runs them at once: 800 ms at p50 instead of 1,550. Retrieval needs the rejection code, so it still waits.

steps.title: Cap the slow tool
steps.text: The exchange log has a long tail: p95 2,400 ms. A 1.5 s timeout caps it; the 8% of calls that run over get an answer built from order status and margin, and the function returns a flag so fallbacks are counted, not hidden.

steps.title: Cut an LLM hop
steps.text: The separate intent call (600 / 900 ms) is gone: the app already knows the question type from the button, so the answer call reads the question itself. The longer prompt adds about 100 ms. First words at p95: 1.5 + 0.2 + 0.9 = 2.6 s; total p95: 1.5 + 0.2 + 3.3 = 5.0 s. Both budgets are met.

pros: Turns “make it faster” into targets anyone can check on a dashboard
Shows which stage to fix first instead of guessing
Streaming and status lines cut abandonment even before real latency falls
Parallel calls and fewer LLM hops cut real time without new hardware
cons: Tracing every stage takes instrumentation work up front
Timeouts turn some answers into degraded ones that must be designed and labelled
Merging LLM calls makes prompts longer and harder to test
Streaming complicates output guardrails, which must check text in flight
avoidWhen: Batch or overnight jobs where nobody waits on the answer (optimise cost instead)
A single short model call with no tools, where the serving layer sets almost all the latency

playgroundGuide.scenario: Tejas Trade, a fictional stockbroking app, answers “why did my order fail?” about 10,000 times a day. Each answer needs an intent step, three tool calls (order status 300 ms, margin check 450 ms, exchange rejection log 800 ms at p50, with a 2,400 ms p95 tail), a 150 ms help search that needs the rejection code, and a 2,400 ms answer call whose first token arrives at 500 ms. The budget at p95: first words within 3 s, the full answer within 5.5 s, and no more than 10% of answers degraded by a fallback.
controls: Choose how the intent step runs: a separate large-model call, a separate small fast model, or merged into the answer call.
Tick parallel tool calls, and choose what the user sees while waiting: a spinner, streamed tokens, or a status line plus tokens.
Set the timeout on the slow exchange log, or load a scenario.

outputs.name: First visible text
outputs.meaning: When anything useful appears on screen at p50 and p95: a status line, the first words or the whole answer.

outputs.name: First answer words
outputs.meaning: When the answer itself starts to appear; the budget is 3 s at p95.

outputs.name: Total
outputs.meaning: When the answer is complete at p50 and p95; the budget is 5.5 s at p95. Stage p95s are added, a deliberately cautious estimate.

outputs.name: Users who give up
outputs.meaning: An illustrative abandonment model: 4% per second of blank screen after the first second, 2% per second of waiting for words once something is visible.

outputs.name: Answers degraded by the fallback
outputs.meaning: Answers built without the exchange’s reason because the exchange log hit the timeout.

presets.name: Everything in turn, spinner
presets.expect: Nothing visible until 4.7 s (7.7 s at p95). Both budgets missed; about 14.8% of users, 1,480 a day, give up.

presets.name: Stream the tokens only
presets.expect: First words at 2.8 s (5.3 s at p95), total still 4.7 / 7.7 s. Abandonment halves to 7.2%, 720 a day, but both budgets are still missed.

presets.name: Merged, parallel, status, 1.5 s timeout
presets.expect: Status at 0.3 s, first words 1.55 s (2.6 s at p95), total 3.45 s (5.0 s at p95). 1.1% give up (110 a day); 8% of answers, 800 a day, fall back. Inside the budget.

presets.name: Same, with a 1 s timeout
presets.expect: Total p95 drops to 4.5 s and first words to 2.1 s, but 20% of answers, 2,000 a day, lose the exchange’s reason: over the 10% limit.

missions.text: Meet the whole budget: first words ≤ 3 s and total ≤ 5.5 s at p95, with at most 10% of answers degraded.
missions.hint: Stream, run the tools in parallel and use a 1,500 ms timeout; then either merge the intent step or use the small model.

missions.text: Get abandonment to 4% or less while the p50 total stays at 4.5 s or more: perceived latency, not real latency.
missions.hint: Keep the large intent call and sequential tools, but show a status line at once and stream the tokens.

missions.text: Show how an over-tight timeout buys speed with thinner answers: total p95 under 5 s but more than 10% degraded.
missions.hint: Merge the intent step, run tools in parallel and set the timeout to 1,000 ms.

tools.best: Standard span names and attributes for model calls, tools and agents, so every stage lands in one trace.
tools.ex: Emit a span per LLM call, tool and retrieval and chart p50 and p95 per span name in your existing observability stack.

tools.best: LLM tracing with nested spans, time to first token and latency percentiles per step.
tools.ex: Trace each “why did my order fail?” request and compare p95 of the answer span before and after merging the intent call.
pros: LLM-aware views out of the box
cons: Another service to run or pay for

tools.best: gather for independent calls, wait_for for a timeout on one slow call.
tools.ex: Run order status, margin and exchange log together and cap the exchange log at 1.5 s.
cons: No tracing or retries by itself

tools.best: Anthropic, OpenAI and Gemini APIs send tokens as server-sent events as they are generated.
tools.ex: Forward text deltas from the answer call to the app so the first words show at about 0.5 s into the call.
pros: Large cut in time to first words
cons: Output guardrails must work on partial text

tools.ex: Show “Checking your order…” as a data part, then the streamed answer, in a Next.js support page.

quickPicks.need: Parallel calls and timeouts in Python

goals: Write a latency budget as p95 targets and measure each stage against it
Calculate first words and total time for sequential, parallel and merged designs
Explain the trade-off between a tighter timeout and degraded answers

practice.scenario: Tejas Trade, a fictional stockbroking app, has an assistant that answers “why did my order fail?”. The first version made an intent call, three tool calls one after another, a help-article search and an answer call, and showed a spinner for 4.7 s (7.7 s at p95). The team set a budget of first words within 3 s and the full answer within 5.5 s at p95, traced every stage, and then streamed a status line and tokens, ran the tools in parallel, dropped the intent call and put a 1.5 s timeout on the slow exchange log. The p95 total fell to 5.0 s and first words to 2.6 s, with 8% of answers built without the exchange’s reason.

industries.use: Order, UPI and payout “what happened?” questions that must answer before the user retries or calls support
Bill and recharge assistants that stream a status line while plan and usage lookups run in parallel
Order-tracking chat where a slow courier API is capped by a timeout and answered from the last known scan

practice.analogy: A restaurant kitchen at dinner rush. The waiter brings water and bread at once (the status line), the chef cooks the dal, rice and sabzi on three burners together (parallel calls), nobody takes the order twice (one LLM hop), and if the tandoor is backed up the table is offered a different bread rather than a forty-minute wait (timeout and fallback).

library.name: Anthropic Python SDK
library.what: AsyncAnthropic streams a message as it is generated; asyncio runs the tool calls in parallel and times out the slow one.

practice.note: The tool functions are stubs that sleep for their p50 times. The model id is an example; use one available to your account. The same pattern works with any provider that streams over server-sent events.

samples.code:
import asyncio, time
from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic

client = AsyncAnthropic()                     # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
MODEL = "claude-haiku-4-5"                    # example id: a fast model for this path

async def order_status(oid):  await asyncio.sleep(0.30); return {"code": "RMS_MARGIN", "state": "rejected"}
async def margin_check(oid):  await asyncio.sleep(0.45); return {"shortfall_inr": 1840}
async def exchange_log(oid):  await asyncio.sleep(0.80); return {"reason": "Insufficient margin at RMS"}
async def search_help(code):  await asyncio.sleep(0.15); return ["Why orders are rejected for margin"]

async def capped(coro, seconds, fallback):
    try:
        return await asyncio.wait_for(coro, timeout=seconds)
    except asyncio.TimeoutError:
        return fallback

async def why_failed(oid, question):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    print("[status] Checking your order…", flush=True)            # visible at once
    status, margin, log = await asyncio.gather(                   # parallel tools
        order_status(oid), margin_check(oid),
        capped(exchange_log(oid), 1.5, {"reason": None, "degraded": True}))
    docs = await search_help(log["reason"] or status["code"])     # needs the code
    prompt = (f"Question: {question}\nOrder: {status}\nMargin: {margin}\n"
              f"Exchange: {log}\nHelp: {docs}\n"
              "Explain in two sentences why the order failed and what to do. "
              "If the exchange reason is missing, say so.")
    first = None
    async with client.messages.stream(model=MODEL, max_tokens=300,
                                      messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]) as stream:
        async for text in stream.text_stream:                     # one hop, streamed
            if first is None:
                first = time.perf_counter() - t0
            print(text, end="", flush=True)
    total = time.perf_counter() - t0
    print(f"\nfirst words {first:.2f} s · total {total:.2f} s · degraded {log.get('degraded', False)}")

asyncio.run(why_failed("ORD-5521", "Why did my order fail?"))

numericDrill.question: An assistant makes a 600 ms intent call, then three independent tool calls of 300, 450 and 800 ms, then a 150 ms retrieval, then a streamed answer call whose first token arrives 500 ms after it starts. If the tools run in parallel, when do the first answer words appear, in milliseconds?
numericDrill.answer: 600 + max(300, 450, 800) + 150 + 500 = 600 + 800 + 150 + 500 = 2,050 ms. With the tools in turn it would be 600 + 1,550 + 150 + 500 = 2,800 ms, and without streaming the user would wait for the whole answer.

interview.question: How would you set and enforce a latency budget for an LLM feature?
interview.answer: Agree targets with the product owner at p95, for example first words within 3 s and the full answer within 5.5 s. Trace every stage (each LLM call, tool and retrieval) and record p50 and p95. Find the critical path, then remove waits: stream early, run independent calls in parallel, merge or shrink LLM hops, and cap slow dependencies with timeouts and planned fallbacks. Alert when a stage’s p95 drifts past its share of the budget.

interview.question: Streaming made users happier but the total time did not change. Was it worth it?
interview.answer: Yes, within limits. Perceived latency depends mostly on when something useful appears; a status line and streamed words cut abandonment even at the same total. But the total still matters for users who need the whole answer, and streaming cannot hide a 7 s p95. Treat streaming as the first fix, not the only one.

mistakes.mistake: Budgeting on the average response time
mistakes.fix: Set p95 targets per stage and end to end; the slow tail is where users leave

mistakes.mistake: Adding a tight timeout and not counting fallbacks
mistakes.fix: Track the share of degraded answers and budget it like latency

quiz.question: A trading app’s assistant averages 2.1 s per answer, but its p95 is 7.7 s and support tickets say it “hangs”. What should the latency budget be written against?
options: The p95 (or p99), per stage and end to end
The fastest answer of the day
quiz.explanation: Users who leave sit in the slow tail. Budgets are written and checked at p95 or p99, not the mean.

quiz.question: Stages in turn: intent 600 ms, tools 1,550 ms, retrieval 150 ms, answer 2,400 ms. With no streaming, when does the user see any text?
quiz.explanation: 600 + 1,550 + 150 + 2,400 = 4,700 ms. Without streaming, the first visible text is the whole answer.

quiz.question: The answer call takes 2,400 ms and its first token arrives at 500 ms. Everything before it takes 2,300 ms. With streaming, when do the first words appear?
quiz.explanation: 2,300 + 500 = 2,800 ms, 1,900 ms sooner than waiting for the full answer.

quiz.question: A recharge assistant calls three independent APIs taking 300, 450 and 800 ms. How long does that step take if they run in parallel?
quiz.explanation: Parallel calls take as long as the slowest: 800 ms, against 1,550 ms in turn.

quiz.question: Which changes shorten the real end-to-end time of an order-tracking assistant, not just how it feels? Select all that apply.
options: Running independent tool calls in parallel
Merging a separate intent call into the answer call
Showing a “Checking your order…” status line
Using a faster model for an early classification step
quiz.explanation: A status line improves perceived latency only; the other three remove waiting from the critical path.

quiz.question: A claims assistant shows a spinner for 5 s, then the whole answer. Which single change cuts abandonment most with the least work?
options: Streaming a status line and the answer tokens
quiz.explanation: Streaming shows progress within the first second and words as soon as the first token arrives, with no change to the pipeline.

quiz.question: An exchange-log API has a p50 of 800 ms and a p95 of 2,400 ms; 8% of calls exceed 1.5 s. With a 1.5 s timeout and fallback, what is that step’s p95 and the share of degraded answers?
quiz.explanation: More than 5% of calls hit the cap, so the p95 becomes 1,500 ms, and those 8% of answers are built without the log.

quiz.question: A team tightens a slow tool’s timeout from 1.5 s to 1 s. p95 improves by 500 ms, but degraded answers rise from 8% to 20% of 10,000 a day. How many more degraded answers is that each day?
quiz.explanation: 20% − 8% = 12% of 10,000 = 1,200 more degraded answers a day.

quiz.question: Which belong in a latency budget for a patient-portal assistant? Select all that apply.
options: A p95 target for first visible words
A p95 target for the full answer
A maximum share of answers that may fall back
The GPU model used by the provider
quiz.explanation: The budget is written in user terms: first words, total time and how many answers may degrade. Hardware is not the user’s concern.

quiz.question: An NBFC’s loan assistant makes three LLM calls in a row: classify (700 ms), plan (1,200 ms) and answer (2,500 ms). Classify only picks one of five intents. What is the cheapest cut?
options: Replace classify with a small fast model or a rule, or fold it into the plan call
Run all three LLM calls in parallel
Add a cache in front of the answer call only
Use a bigger model for classify
quiz.explanation: An early step with a simple job can use a faster model or merge into the next call; the plan and answer depend on each other, so they cannot run in parallel.

quiz.question: Sequential stage p95s are 900, 3,400, 200 and 3,200 ms. Using the cautious rule of adding stage p95s, what is the end-to-end p95 estimate?
quiz.explanation: 900 + 3,400 + 200 + 3,200 = 7,700 ms. Adding p95s overstates the true p95 slightly, which is the safe side for a budget.

quiz.question: Retrieval needs the rejection code returned by the exchange log. Can it run in parallel with the three tool calls?
options: Yes, always run everything in parallel
No, it depends on one tool’s output, so it must wait for it
Only if the model is streaming
quiz.explanation: Parallelism applies to independent calls. A step that needs another’s output stays after it on the critical path.

quiz.question: An assistant streams tokens. Which new problems must the team handle? Select all that apply.
options: Output guardrails must check text while it is still arriving
Errors can arrive after some text is already on screen
Clients must render partial text and a final state
quiz.explanation: Streaming does not slow the first token; it changes how checks, errors and rendering work.

quiz.question: Abandonment is modelled as 4% per second of blank screen after the first second. A UPI help bot shows nothing for 4.7 s. What share of users give up?
A trace shows p95 per stage: intent 900 ms, tools 1,500 ms, retrieval 200 ms, answer 3,200 ms. The budget is 5.5 s total at p95. Which change fits the budget without touching the tools?
options: Removing the separate intent call (merging it into the answer)
quiz.explanation: 900 + 1,500 + 200 + 3,200 = 5,800 ms. Dropping the 900 ms hop and adding about 100 ms of prompt to the answer call gives 5,000 ms; faster retrieval saves too little, and streaming or a status line do not change the total.

quiz.question: Why does the tail matter more when an answer fans out to several tools?
options: Each extra dependency adds another chance to hit its slow tail, so the request’s p95 is set by the worst of them
Parallel calls are always slower than sequential ones
Tails cancel out across many calls
Fan-out only affects cost, not latency
quiz.explanation: The tail at scale: the more calls a request waits on, the more likely one of them is slow.

quiz.question: A lab-results assistant answers in 4 s. A status line “Fetching your report…” appears at 0.3 s. What has improved?
options: Perceived latency; the total is unchanged
quiz.explanation: A status line tells the user the system is working. Real latency still needs changes on the critical path.

quiz.question: A “why is my bill high?” assistant misses its budget. Which should you do first? Select all that apply.
options: Trace each LLM call, tool and retrieval and record p50 and p95
Find the stages on the critical path
Switch every stage to the smallest model available
Compare each stage’s p95 with its share of the budget
quiz.explanation: Measure before changing. Shrinking every model blindly can hurt quality without touching the stage that sets the total.

quiz.question: A courier API times out. What should the fallback answer do?
options: Invent a delivery date so the answer looks complete
Answer from the last known scan and say the live status is unavailable
quiz.explanation: A good fallback uses the data that did arrive and states what is missing, so users get facts rather than a confident guess.

quiz.question: Before: first words p95 7.7 s, total p95 7.7 s. After merging the intent call, parallel tools, streaming and a 1.5 s timeout: first words 2.6 s, total 5.0 s. By what percentage did the p95 total fall?
quiz.explanation: (7.7 − 5.0) ÷ 7.7 = 2.7 ÷ 7.7 ≈ 35%. First words fell further, by about 66%, because streaming also moved them earlier.
